title.en: Fourth-power radius scaling checked by ratios

summary: Verify a fourth-power resistance relation with radius ratios, a declared control variable and rejected invalid inputs.
objective: Halving the radius multiplies the computed resistance by sixteen, one independently computed absolute case matches the display, and the panel states which variable is held constant.
applies_when: A model compares an algebraic relation across parameter values rather than simulating flow.
The relation contains a high power that makes unit and radius-versus-diameter mistakes invisible in a single number.
A viewer can move a parameter toward zero or a nonphysical value.
intent_signals: check the radius exponent in this resistance demo
is it holding flow or pressure constant
example_prompts: Check the fourth-power radius behaviour of this vessel resistance comparison.

principles: Ratios and absolute values check different things: a ratio isolates the exponent while cancelling every constant factor, so a radius-for-diameter substitution, which shifts the result by a factor of sixteen and leaves the exponent at minus four, is invisible to ratios and needs one independently computed absolute case.
A comparison needs a declared control variable: holding volume flow constant and holding pressure difference constant give different visible answers, and a display implying both is wrong.
Inputs have a valid domain; radius, length and viscosity must be positive and finite, and zero radius is a division by zero rather than an infinitely resistive vessel to draw.
implementation: Compute resistance from the declared tube relation with all inputs in one consistent unit system, and print the units beside every number.

Evaluate resistance ratios for the radius pairs r and half r, and r and double r, at fixed length and viscosity, then compare resistance across several radii on a logarithmic scale to read the exponent.

Compute one absolute case by hand from a stated radius, length and viscosity with their units and compare it with the displayed value, and state whether the input field is a radius or a diameter, because that substitution shifts the absolute value by a factor of sixteen without moving the exponent.
Run both modes explicitly, fixed pressure difference with flow derived and fixed flow with pressure difference derived, and label which variable is held in each panel.
Feed the boundary and invalid inputs: zero radius, negative viscosity, a non-numeric entry, and a radius small enough to overflow the reciprocal.
observable_checks: Halving the radius multiplies computed resistance by sixteen and doubling divides it by sixteen, within the default tolerance rule (knowledge.validation-default-tolerance-rule) unless this record states its own; for well-conditioned finite inputs in the normal double-precision range this arithmetic stays accurate far beyond one part in a million, so a visible deviation there is a modelling error rather than roundoff. That expectation does not extend to the deliberately extreme inputs below.

The exponent read from the logarithmic comparison is minus four within the same tolerance; a value near minus two means the modelled dependence itself is wrong, an area-like square instead of the fourth power, since a radius-for-diameter substitution would leave this slope unchanged.
The independently computed absolute case matches the displayed value with matching units, and the panel states whether its input is a radius or a diameter.

Nonpositive or non-numeric inputs are rejected with a message, extreme inputs that overflow the reciprocal are reported as out of range rather than shown as a number, and no panel presents both flow and pressure difference as held constant at the same time.

known_limits: Checks an ideal steady laminar rigid-tube relation; it makes no claim about blood, compliant vessels or any clinical prediction.
Authored verification guidance; no computation was run for this record.
creative_affordances: Adapt the scenario, scale and presentation to your subject; this record fixes what must be checked, not how the scene must look.

claims.statement: In the ideal tube relation resistance equals eight times viscosity times length divided by pi times the fourth power of the radius, so a vessel constricting to half its radius increases resistance sixteen times.
claims.scope: Steady laminar Newtonian flow in an ideal cylindrical tube as presented in the cited physiology section; real vessels and blood need further assumptions.

source_refs.locator: Poiseuille equation, rearranged resistance equation and the one-half radius example
